chapter: Life in France and Sidney Bechet
title: Sitting in with Sidney Bechet's band at the Vieux Colombier
summary: Urged to visit Bechet in Paris, Waters borrowed Claude Luter's soprano, played so well the crowd roared, and Bechet through Jacques Butler banned him from the club out of jealousy.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: Another question on your being in France here in the '50's. A few years before you went over another reed player, someone who you'd known all along, Sidney Bechet, had gone over.
Yeah.
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82 91
Did you ever - first of all, did you ever meet up with Sidney over there?
Yeah, sure. I was first -
Could you talk about yourself and Sidney Bechet in France, whenever you were -

Yeah, I'll give you the one instance that I remember real well about Sidney Bechet. Which is, if it's not true Jacques Butler told me. When I was living with Henry Goodwin's mother - see, [ ], 19th Street and Seventh Avenue, I was living with her. He wasn't there but I was living with her, his mother. So she knew Sidney 'cause Sidney, they stayed at her house when he visited New York at one time. So she knew that I was going, so she said "Be sure to go around to see Sidney". So Sidney at that time was working at the Vieux Colombier, which was where, he stayed there for a long time. So he was workin' up there with Claude Luter, a little club there with amateur musicians at that period, see, Sidney was the big star. See, so I go up there. When I go up there Claude Luter asked me to play the sax, to borrow the saxophone, his soprano saxophone. I go up there to see Bechet, not to play. He kept on insisting, see, so - and I said I wasn't digging. See, if I mean, 'cause I knew that something gonna turn up like it did I would refues. Well, finally he kept on insisting so I took his saophone, borrowed his saxophone and played real easy, you know? And that's unusual for a mouthpiece, that's [ ] - "Oh, maybe I will", [ ], see. So I played one of those old jazz standards like "Back Home Again In Indiana", you know I mean?
Sure.
I played the hell out of that because I just left Jimmy Archey's, you know what I mean?
Right, you'd been playing soprano, right -

You know, I was - you ask these guys about anything, I could play the damn thing. I was playing real good soprano, see. Yes, he asked that guy who, very great soprano player around here, the guy that used to -
Bob Wilber -
Not Bob, the one that used to work with Bob Wilber, they called it the ["Soprano Summit"] -
Oh, Kenny Davern -
Kenny - ask Kenny, he'll tell you -
"Soprano Summit" -
He'd come down the stairs and listen to me, at least that's what he told me in
Benny Waters, JOHP 6/6/82

London. I was wailing on soprano, I really - that is when I was wailing on that, that period, see. So I picked up the horn and played so good and I wailin' and people applaud like a fool, they were crazy, you know? And it's Sidney Bechet's job - that's his job, you know. So the people screamed, then after I only appeared in one number, see, then I stopped, see. The very next Monday was a day off for Sidney and he came down to La Cigalle where I was working with Jimmy - with Jacques -
PS: Jacques Butler.

He told Jacques Butler 'You tell that little son of a so-and-so, don't come up [to] my place no more', you know what I mean? That's true, I mean it's natural, that's what Jacques Butler told me - jealousy, you know.
PS: So you didn't see Bechet too much after that.
